items.name: Melba Liston
items.description: American jazz trombonist, musical arranger, and composer (1926–1999)

witness_rows.one_liner: wrote his arrangements for forty years
witness_rows.summary: Liston recalled meeting Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie, said she had arranged his music with complete freedom from ’56 to ’96, and thanked him for pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
witness_rows.lead_quote: I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.
witness_rows.caution: 'because nobody else did' is her view after the stroke; in the next turn she names Frank and other arrangers as friends, so it should not be read as an accusation against named people. Many Weston lines in this interview are the interviewer Clora Bryant's ('Randy is your horn right now', the recording dates, 'in different clothing') and must not be attributed to Liston. '[Weston]' in 'Randy [Weston]' is the transcriber's bracket. 'He don’t tell me anything' (295901) means he gives her free rein, not that he is uncommunicative; do not show it without the freedom context.
witness_rows.doc_title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

he_said.one_liner: his arranger; wrote left-handed after her stroke
he_said.summary: Weston said only Melba Liston could arrange “Spirit of Our Ancestors”, told how he goaded her back to work after her stroke — she learned to write music on a computer with her left hand — and recalled her arrangements arriving from a California hospital in time for the 1959 Five Spot date and the 1985 Montreal concert.
he_said.his_quote: I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know?

witness_rows.one_liner: toured europe with him while on dialysis
witness_rows.summary: Powell said every time Weston sat down at the piano it sounded like a concerto, called him the most scholarly person he knew, and told how his boss arranged his dialysis on European tours and offered to carry his bags.
witness_rows.lead_quote: It sounds like a concerto every time he sits down. It’s amazing.

Powell's biographical asides (lives in Marrakesh and Brooklyn, 'working with the United Nations', 'living in Africa ... 30 years') are unverified and should not be lifted. 'the greatest pianist in the world' trails off into a self-correction about practising; do not quote it bare.

witness_rows.one_liner: went to morocco to film his return
witness_rows.summary: Powell said fifteen years in Weston's band had been glorious, recalled the trip to Morocco to film his return there, and quoted him as wanting 'to put the magic back in music', calling him a spellbinder who leads by example and pays well.
witness_rows.lead_quote: he said, “I’m just trying to put the magic back in music.” And boy can he ever do it. He is a spellbinder.
witness_rows.caution: In the Morocco story Powell runs the Gnawa together with the village he calls 'Joujouka' and names 'Brian Smith' of the Rolling Stones (Brian Jones); his dating of Weston's father's words and first Tangier visit ('maybe 25 years ago') is loose. Do not lift those details into captions. The title says Monk Rowe, but this first interview was conducted by Michael Woods.
witness_rows.doc_title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

items.name: Jon Hendricks
items.description: American jazz singer, lyricist, jazz critic and historian (1921–2017)

witness_rows.one_liner: wrote a church-song lyric to his tune
witness_rows.summary: Hendricks said he admired and worked with Weston when he arrived on the scene, set his 'Blues for Strayhorn' as a church song, and placed him in a line of depth running from Duke Ellington through Monk.
witness_rows.lead_quote: Randy Weston also has depth, because he comes from Monk, which is the lineage Duke – Monk – Randy. So he has some of that depth.
witness_rows.caution: 'some of that depth' ranks him just below Duke and Monk; the next sentence in the second block ('At that time he did all of what I consider his best tunes') implies his later work was weaker, so do not extend the second quote. Check that 'Blues for Strayhorn' is the title of a Weston composition before naming it. The interviewer, not Hendricks, mentions lyrics to Little Niles and Hi-Fly.

he_said.one_liner: pipa master; recorded the shang with him
he_said.summary: Weston met the pipa master Min Xiao Fen in Atlanta, heard her play at his Brooklyn home, went with her to the Guggenheim to study the Shang dynasty, and recorded her composition 'The Shang' with her on 'Khepera'.
he_said.his_quote: So, it turned out she was living in Brooklyn, at that particular time, so she came by my house and she took out the pipa and she started to play. It was so beautiful I said, “We have to play together.”

he_said.one_liner: dear friend; got him the alexandria library opening
he_said.summary: Weston called Salah Ragab, a Cairo big-band leader who played Duke and Basie, a dear friend whose death he learned of only months later, and said Ragab got him invited to play the opening of the new library in Alexandria.
he_said.his_quote: Yeah, a dear friend of mine, in fact he died last year and I didn’t find out until two months ago, his name is Salah Ragab.

he_said.one_liner: the human contact that shaped his piano
he_said.summary: Weston said he plays the piano the way he does because he had human contact with Thelonious Monk, whom he counted among the royalty of piano he grew up with.
he_said.his_quote: I play the piano like I play because I had the human contact with Thelonious Monk, because I had the spiritual contact with Nat King Cole, who I never met.

he_said.summary: Weston said the young Gnawa Abdullah Al-Gourd, who worked for Voice of America and spoke English, was his first contact with the Gnawa in 1967 and led him to the old masters, and he led the Tangier Gnawa at Weston's Brooklyn church concert.
he_said.his_quote: Abdullah Al-Gourd, he was very interested in the history of his people. Because of him, I recorded and I met some of the old Gnawa.

witness_rows.one_liner: recommended him for the africa trip
witness_rows.summary: Taylor recalled that he and Weston, both recording for Riverside, were fascinated by its African field recordings, that he recommended Weston for an early-1960s cultural trip to Africa when he could not go, and called him a remarkable musician who had gone back to the roots as few others had.
witness_rows.lead_quote: Randy Weston is a remarkable musician who has over the years taken the historical line from Africa that has been developed in the Americas and has done something very special with it.
witness_rows.caution: The second quote compresses history: 'this is when Randy first went to Africa and he ultimately stayed there' is Taylor's recollection; the trip and his later residence in Africa were years apart, and the claim that Taylor's recommendation sent him is Taylor's alone. In 317235 the transcript garbles the name as 'Randy Western' (Monk and 'Randy Western' as spare pianists); if that line is used, correct with [sic] or editorial note.
witness_rows.doc_title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

he_said.one_liner: his wife; married in a nubian village ceremony
he_said.summary: Weston said he met his wife Fatoumata Mbengue, a Lebou/Wolof woman from Senegal with an African shop in Paris, through Gnawa who invited her to his Paris concert, and that he suddenly declared he wanted to marry her in Egypt, where they wed in a Nubian ceremony.
he_said.his_quote: Well, what happened was, I met my wife, Fatoumata Mbengue. She’s a Lebo woman, Wulluf, from Senegal. She has a beautiful African shop in Paris.
he_said.era: married after his NEA Jazz Masters award

witness_rows.one_liner: got an inch-thick stack of his lead sheets
witness_rows.summary: Owens credited Weston, with Donald Byrd, for teaching him to keep his own publishing, and recalled Weston handing him an inch-thick stack of lead sheets at a musicians' meeting on 135th Street with the advice to write his music out if he wanted it recorded.
witness_rows.lead_quote: Randy Weston gave me a stack of about an inch of his lead sheets. One of the things he said was, “You’ve gotta have your stuff written out if you want people to record it.”
witness_rows.doc_title: Jimmy Owens — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

witness_rows.one_liner: learned the publishing business from him
witness_rows.summary: Owens named Weston, after Donald Byrd, as one of his mentors and said Weston taught him how music publishing works, knowledge that led him into teaching the business of music.
witness_rows.lead_quote: Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works.
witness_rows.doc_title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

he_said.one_liner: taxi driver who threw out the seat
he_said.summary: Weston said the Egyptian taxi driver Ramsey, whom he would never forget, threw out the taxi's seat to give him legroom and broke away from the tourist convoy to drive him and Fatou to Aswan.
he_said.his_quote: We talked to the taxi cab driver to take us, Ramsey, I’ll never forget him. He took the seat out of the taxi and made sure I had a lot of legroom, he threw the whole seat out!

he_said.summary: Weston said Shadley, an inspector of antiquities who approached him and Fatou at the temple of Isis in Aswan, showed them round and introduced them to the head of the Nubian museum, and on a later trip arranged their Nubian wedding when Weston suddenly told him he wanted to marry her.

items.description: Randy Weston's father, who taught him African history and made him take piano lessons

he_said.one_liner: taught him african history; made him play piano
he_said.summary: Weston said his father taught him to study African civilization from before slavery, kept maps of African kings and queens and books by African historians in their Brooklyn home, told him he was an African born in America, and made him take piano lessons.
he_said.his_quote: My father taught me to study African civilization when Africa was great. Most of us get the education of Africa, Africa after slavery, that’s where we start.

items.name: Weston's sister (unnamed)
items.description: Randy Weston's only sibling, five years older, who died in 2001 and was buried in Brooklyn on 11 September 2001

he_said.one_liner: his older sister, buried on 9-11
he_said.summary: Weston said his only sister, five years older, was his protector as a child, strong, spiritual and giving with a great sense of humour, and that she died in 2001 and was buried at Evergreen Cemetery on 11 September 2001 as the smoke from the World Trade Center was visible.
he_said.his_quote: I have one sister, no brothers. My sister was five years older than me. She was my boss, you know? When I was younger, despite my physical size, if anybody messed with me I’d get my sister. She was strong but very spiritual, very giving.

he_said.summary: Weston said Riverside wanted his first record to be solo piano, he wanted a trio, and they compromised on a duo with Sam Gill on bass for the Cole Porter album.
he_said.his_quote: Finally, we compromised with myself and Sam Gill on bass. So, my first recording of Cole Porter was piano and bass, but they wanted me to do solo piano.

witness_rows.one_liner: had him in the studio before monk
witness_rows.summary: Keepnews named Weston among the easygoing artists he had been in the studio with before Thelonious Monk, and said Cannonball Adderley's live album carried what he believed was the first recording of Weston's 'Hi-Fly'.
witness_rows.lead_quote: before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats.
witness_rows.caution: 'all pussycats' means easy to work with, set against Monk as 'a real tough cookie'; shown bare it can read as belittling. The second quote's claim that Cannonball's was the first recording of 'Hi-Fly' is Keepnews's own hedge ('as far as I know') and is probably wrong: Weston recorded the tune himself before Cannonball's 1959 live album (check discography before printing). 'High Fly' is the transcript's spelling of Hi-Fly. The 'waltz king' remark in the same block is Cannonball's on-record patter, reported, not Keepnews's judgement.
witness_rows.doc_title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

witness_rows.one_liner: had his albums on the office wall

witness_rows.lead_quote: he said, “Oh, Randy! I’m glad somebody got around to recording him. It should have been done along time ago,”
witness_rows.caution: The praise in the lead is Miles Davis's, reported by Keepnews; caption it as Miles's remark, not Keepnews's judgement. 'along time ago' is verbatim.

he_said.one_liner: duke's sister, who only wanted his solo piano
he_said.summary: Weston said Duke Ellington's sister Ruth Ellington only wanted to hear him play solo piano and would not hear him any other way.
he_said.his_quote: Duke Ellington’s sister, Ruth Ellington; she didn’t want to hear me any other way.

he_said.one_liner: prayed with the band for his sister
he_said.summary: Weston named TK Blue in his bands from the 1985 Montreal ten-piece through the 1997 residency, the Brooklyn church concert and St. Lucia, and recalled him and “the guys” coming to the church to pray for his sister the day before her burial in 2001.
he_said.his_quote: Exactly, but the day before TK Blue and the guys came to the church and they all prayed for my sister in the church.

he_said.one_liner: bassist who rode a donkey up to jajouka
he_said.summary: Weston, having forgotten the bass player of the sextet he took to Morocco, later remembered him as Tom McKenzie while describing the band riding donkeys up the mountain to Jajouka.
he_said.his_quote: Tom McKenzie was the bass player. Seeing these guys going up the mountains on these donkeys, with their instruments, that was incredible.

he_said.one_liner: his book inspired the record ancient future
he_said.summary: Weston said Chandler's book 'Ancient Future', on ancient contact between Africa and China, inspired his solo record of that name; Chandler showed him photographs of ancient Chinese masks.
he_said.his_quote: That wonderful book that Dr. Wayne Chandler wrote, which says that in order for us to go ahead we have got to go back.

he_said.one_liner: gave up on him after three years
he_said.summary: Weston recalled, on receiving the NEA Jazz Masters award, that his piano teacher had given up on him after three years and told his father to save his money.
he_said.his_quote: This is the guy that the piano teacher gave up on after three years. He told my father to save his money!

items.name: Weston's mother (unnamed)
items.description: Randy Weston's mother, who took him to church every Sunday; a member of the People's Institutional Church in Brooklyn

he_said.one_liner: gave him the black church every sunday
he_said.summary: Weston said that while his father made him take piano lessons his mother gave him the black church, which he had to attend every Sunday, and he marvelled at how his parents kept the family spiritual and loving despite poverty and racism.
he_said.his_quote: My father made me take piano lessons and my mother gave me black church. I had to be there every Sunday.

he_said.one_liner: arranged his canterbury performance with three gnawa
he_said.summary: Weston said a woman from India, Zeba Rachman, arranged for him and three Gnawa from Tangiers to play for a meeting of spiritual leaders at Canterbury.
he_said.his_quote: Well, that was organized by a woman from India, Zeba…

he_said.one_liner: played oud on his 1974 european tour
he_said.summary: Weston named Abdul-Malik on oud in his 1974 European touring group and among the musicians at the festival he organised in Tangier in 1972.
he_said.his_quote: I had Ahmed Abdul- Malik on the oud; I had William Allen on bass, myself at the piano, Steve Berrios on percussion cause my son couldn’t make it. We toured, the first time, to play Europe.

he_said.one_liner: met in the berkshires summers
he_said.summary: Weston said he met Foss in the Berkshires through the Boston Symphony Orchestra milieu and spoke of “my original recording with Bernstein and Lucas”, the waltzes for children.
he_said.his_quote: I met people like Luckas Foss and Leonard Bernstein.

he_said.one_liner: records he played at his tangier club
he_said.summary: Weston said that at his African Rhythms club in Tangier he played records of Marvin Gaye, among others, so that young Moroccans could hear the real African American music rather than European imitations.
he_said.his_quote: We had singers from the Congo…we played records of James Brown, Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, Ray Charles, so the young Moroccans could hear our real music cause they were getting imitations of our music from Europe; they weren’t hearing the real thing.

he_said.summary: Weston listed Bin Fata in his ten-piece group at the 1985 Montreal Jazz Festival, apparently as the Gnawa member playing African percussion.
he_said.his_quote: I had a ten-piece group of the great Benny Bailey, Sahib Shihab, TK Blue, Clyde Lucas on drums, Mohammad Bin Fata, the Gnawa playing African percussion, myself on piano, Woodward Little was on bass.

he_said.one_liner: senegalese bandleader min xiao fen worked with
he_said.summary: Weston said that when he met Min Xiao Fen in Atlanta she was working in the multinational group of a Senegalese musician he called 'Mortiem'.
he_said.his_quote: I met her in Atlanta, Georgia and she was working with a Senegalese named Mortiem.

he_said.one_liner: chief of the marrakech gnawa
he_said.summary: Weston named M'Barek Ben Othman as the chief of the Marrakech Gnawa, whom he met a year or two after 1967, apparently among the six Gnawa at the Brooklyn concert.
he_said.his_quote: Abdullah from Tangiers, Marrakech, and the chief is M’Barek Ben Othman. I met him one or two years later.

he_said.one_liner: brought to his 1972 tangier festival
he_said.summary: Weston said that for the three-day festival he organized in Tangier in 1972 he brought over Odetta, alongside Max Roach's band without Max and others.
he_said.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
